content: The methodology employed in this guideline involved the preparation of evidence profiles for preselected topics, utilizing up-to-date systematic reviews. The guideline development group was composed of subject matter experts, methodologists, and representatives of potential stakeholders and consumers. A technical consultation, organized by the WHO and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), was held in Atlanta, USA, from August 13–15, 2012. This meeting aimed to address priority questions regarding the genetic, biological, behavioral, and contextual determinants of folate status in women of reproductive age, as well as the strengths and limitations of current methods for assessing folate status indicators, folate intake, and neural tube defect (NTD) prevalence. Discussions also included the relationship between blood folate concentrations, folate intake, and NTD risk based on in vitro and in vivo studies. A formal meeting of the guideline development group took place in Geneva, Switzerland, from September 23–25, 2013, to review the evidence and reach a consensus on recommendations. External reviewers were identified through a public call for comments to ensure proper interpretation of the recommendations. Ten external reviewers provided feedback on the final document, and three additional expert peer reviewers offered technical input. The methodological approach agreed upon by the guideline development group included a combination of narrative reviews, data analysis, modeling, and systematic reviews following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development was also referenced. The evidence base for the association between red blood cell folate concentrations and NTD risk was considered low in quality, as assessed using the GRADE methodology. The guideline recommends that, at the population level, red blood cell folate concentrations in women of reproductive age should exceed 400 ng/mL (906 nmol/L) to achieve the greatest reduction in NTDs. This threshold can serve as an indicator of folate insufficiency at the population level but cannot predict individual risk for NTD-affected pregnancies. No serum folate threshold is recommended for NTD prevention at the population level. The microbiological assay is recommended as the most reliable method for measuring red blood cell folate concentrations across countries, given its consistency and lack of influence by the MTHFR gene polymorphism. The guideline highlights the importance of improving folate status at the population level through interventions such as folic acid fortification of staple foods or targeted supplementation. It also emphasizes the need for appropriate quality control systems for folate assessment using microbiological assays. The guideline acknowledges that reducing folate insufficiency at the population level may take time, but improvements in red blood cell folate concentrations can lead to reductions in NTD prevalence. Future research priorities include exploring the interactions between red blood cell folate concentrations and conditions such as tuberculosis, HIV, and anti-malarial antifolate drugs; developing field-friendly microbiological assays; and investigating the effects of vitamin B12, altitude, and obesity on folate status and NTD risk. Additionally, research is needed to establish population thresholds for serum folate and to determine the lowest total folate intake required to achieve protective blood folate concentrations against NTDs.
